external_sources.title: PSHE Association: Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Use ground rules, distanced examples, a right to pass and appropriate safeguarding responses.

external_sources.title: FRANK: Alcohol
external_sources.supports: Alcohol can affect judgement and coordination. Mixing alcohol with other drugs can increase harm. These lessons do not supply doses, procurement or use instructions.

external_sources.title: NIAAA: Harmful interactions, mixing alcohol with medicines
external_sources.supports: Alcohol can interact harmfully with medicines. A pharmacist or prescriber can advise; pupils should not change prescribed treatment based on a classroom activity.

external_sources.title: NHS: Poisoning
external_sources.supports: Possible poisoning, unconsciousness or severe breathing problems need emergency help. Do not make a person vomit or give food or drink after suspected poisoning. Follow emergency-service instructions.

external_sources.title: Childline: Asking an adult for help
external_sources.supports: Choose a trusted adult, plan a message, use speech or a note, and seek another adult if needed. Adults may need to share a safety concern with people who can help.

evidence.description: An individual fact-to-risk explanation, a safer choice for a substance-related fictional case, and a refusal/help request with an appropriate support route.
evidence.status: contribution to source assessment; no completion claim

routes.Supported: Supported: work through cases A and B.
routes.Aspire: Aspire: challenge a claim using a fact.

vocab.definition: A substance that can affect the body or brain.
A drug used to treat or prevent illness.
A drug found in some drinks.
A chance that harm could happen.
Saying or showing that you do not agree.
A trained expert who advises on medicines.

cases.text: A friend offers an unknown tablet and says it is safe.
cases.next_step: Decline and tell a trusted adult.
cases.staff_note: No real tablets or realistic handling activity. “Only a little” is not a safe way to identify a substance.

cases.text: A learner has medicine prescribed for them and is unsure about the instructions.
cases.next_step: Ask the authorised adult, pharmacist or prescriber.
cases.staff_note: Medicines can be beneficial. Do not advise stopping, sharing or changing treatment; follow the setting medicines policy.

cases.text: Someone says alcohol cannot affect balance or decisions.
cases.fact: The claim conflicts with health information.
cases.next_step: Use a reliable source; choose a non-alcoholic option.
cases.staff_note: Alcohol can affect coordination and judgement. Do not use intoxication simulations.

cases.text: A person plans to mix alcohol with another drug.
cases.fact: Substances may interact and increase harm.
cases.next_step: Do not mix them; seek qualified advice about medicines.
cases.staff_note: Avoid dosage, combinations or instructions for use. Do not supply adult drinking limits to this age group.

cases.text: Friends pressure Kai to drink. Kai wants to leave with a trusted adult.
cases.fact: Kai has a clear boundary and support route.
cases.next_step: Say no if able, move away and contact the trusted adult.
cases.staff_note: No pupil plays a coercive peer. Adults can read a neutral line; refusal is not the person’s only protection.

cases.text: After taking a substance, a person is unconscious and will not wake.
cases.next_step: Call 999 for an ambulance and get adult help now.
cases.staff_note: Follow the call handler. Do not leave them to sleep it off, give food/drink or make them vomit. No physical demonstration in this lesson.

PSHE-LAUNCH-A2-W04 · Monday 23–Friday 27 November 2026
I Do: 5 minutes.
Teacher: Model each line aloud and make the reasoning explicit. Accept: medicines used as directed can help; unknown tablets cannot be identified by appearance; alcohol can affect judgement/balance; mixing can increase harm. Link the fact to a choice, not a moral judgement. A clear refusal, moving to support or a pharmacist query is valid. Unconsciousness/serious breathing problems need 999; suspected harmful poisoning needs urgent emergency help.

PSHE-LAUNCH-A2-W04 · Monday 23–Friday 27 November 2026
We Do: 5 minutes.
Teacher: Read the hinge aloud, ask for a choice and a reason. C. Appearance and a friend’s reassurance do not establish what a tablet contains or whether it is safe. Do not taste, smell or handle unknown substances. If something harmful may already have been taken, seek urgent medical help; do not wait for this classroom routine. Reteach with an unlabelled container, without a real prop.

The source assessment is retained. This lesson contributes evidence; it does not by itself complete an award. Public award labels are masked only.
Purpose and success checks
How can facts help us make safer choices?
I can explain a drug or alcohol risk. I can use a fact to choose a safer action. I can practise a refusal and a help route.
LAUNCH-PSHE-W4-E1: An individual fact-to-risk explanation, a safer choice for a substance-related fictional case, and a refusal/help request with an appropriate support route.
Before pupils arrive

Read the staff facts and local substance/medicines and safeguarding policies. Print cards and evidence forms. Identify a private support route and who can answer a medicine query. No substances, empty alcohol containers, real medicine packs or tasting/handling props are needed.
Offer processing time, a quiet start and the usual communication support. Capture each learner’s own work. Read the Staff Answers before teaching.
Calendar and continuity

Monday 23–Friday 27 November 2026. One lesson per week on this line. No day or clock slot is inferred; staff enter the actual date above. Use prior vocabulary and the established private-help routine.

Hidden reference for adults.
Hinge and reteach

C. Appearance and a friend’s reassurance do not establish what a tablet contains or whether it is safe. Do not taste, smell or handle unknown substances. If something harmful may already have been taken, seek urgent medical help; do not wait for this classroom routine. Reteach with an unlabelled container, without a real prop.
Access and practice
Supported: work through cases A and B. Independent: explain all six choices. Aspire: challenge a claim using a fact.

Teach the six model facts, then read A–F. Pupils match a fact, risk and action. Rehearse a neutral refusal or question with the adult; nobody pressures a peer. Explain the emergency response plainly without a physical demonstration.

Begin evidence during practice and finish during capture. Accept speech, pointing, drawing, writing or usual AAC. Scribe exact words without supplying the assessed reason. No forced pair work or public performance.
Safe teaching evidence and learner voice
Boundaries

Use third-person cases. Do not ask about pupil or family substance use, medication or diagnoses. No scare images, intoxication role-play, use instructions, doses, procurement or real drug handling. Do not change prescribed treatment. For a live suspected poisoning or emergency, stop the lesson routine and follow emergency procedures.
Assessment and feedback

Accept: medicines used as directed can help; unknown tablets cannot be identified by appearance; alcohol can affect judgement/balance; mixing can increase harm. Link the fact to a choice, not a moral judgement. A clear refusal, moving to support or a pharmacist query is valid. Unconsciousness/serious breathing problems need 999; suspected harmful poisoning needs urgent emergency help.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Lundy moments
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Speaking listening and writing

Explain a claim using a fact, state a boundary, listen to advice and ask a clear support question. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

Model and hinge

A drug can affect the body or brain. Medicines can help when used as directed. Alcohol can affect judgement and balance. Mixing alcohol and other drugs can add harm. An unknown pill cannot be checked by looks. Pause. Ask a trusted adult or pharmacist.

C. Appearance and a friend’s reassurance do not establish what a tablet contains or whether it is safe. Do not taste, smell or handle unknown substances. If something harmful may already have been taken, seek urgent medical help; do not wait for this classroom routine. Reteach with an unlabelled container, without a real prop.
Individual evidence key

Accept: medicines used as directed can help; unknown tablets cannot be identified by appearance; alcohol can affect judgement/balance; mixing can increase harm. Link the fact to a choice, not a moral judgement. A clear refusal, moving to support or a pharmacist query is valid. Unconsciousness/serious breathing problems need 999; suspected harmful poisoning needs urgent emergency help.
Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: No real tablets or realistic handling activity. “Only a little” is not a safe way to identify a substance.
Card B: Medicines can be beneficial. Do not advise stopping, sharing or changing treatment; follow the setting medicines policy.
Card C: Alcohol can affect coordination and judgement. Do not use intoxication simulations.
Card D: Avoid dosage, combinations or instructions for use. Do not supply adult drinking limits to this age group.
Card E: No pupil plays a coercive peer. Adults can read a neutral line; refusal is not the person’s only protection.
Card F: Follow the call handler. Do not leave them to sleep it off, give food/drink or make them vomit. No physical demonstration in this lesson.
Common misunderstandings

Not all drugs are illegal or the same: prescribed medicines can help. A legal product is not automatically harmless. A friend’s confidence or a tablet’s colour does not prove safety. A healthy choice includes getting support; shame and blame can stop people asking for help.
Teaching boundary

Use third-person cases. Do not ask about pupil or family substance use, medication or diagnoses. No scare images, intoxication role-play, use instructions, doses, procurement or real drug handling. Do not change prescribed treatment. For a live suspected poisoning or emergency, stop the lesson routine and follow emergency procedures.
Feedback

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
